lesson.title: Holding it in mind

steps.headline: Holding things in mind for a few seconds

lead.text: While you waited those ten seconds, something kept the digits available. Psychologists call it working memory: the small mental workspace that holds a few pieces of information for a short time while you use them. It is what lets you keep a phone number in mind while you walk across the room to dial it, or hold the start of a sentence while the end of it arrives.

Working memory differs from long-term memory, which holds your knowledge for years and has room for an enormous amount. Working memory is small and easily overwritten. If someone asks you a question before you reach the keypad, the number is often gone.

The size of the store was first estimated in 1956, when the psychologist George Miller gathered results from many experiments and concluded that people can hold about seven items at once, give or take two. That became one of the best-known numbers in psychology, yet it leaves the two lists unexplained. If the limit were seven items, list B would break it as badly as list A does. Something else must set the limit.

The answer turns on what an item is. Later work, notably by the psychologist Nelson Cowan in 2001, looked at what people can hold when they have no chance to repeat the items to themselves or to group them. The limit came out at about four, and the unit being counted is the chunk.

A chunk is a unit you already know as one thing. Someone who has never met the letters R, A and F together sees three separate letters, which make three chunks. A British reader knows RAF as the air force, so for that reader the same letters make a single chunk. The amount of memory used depends on what you know.

Now return to the two lists. List B runs 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 9, a run you know so well that it behaves as one chunk. List A follows no pattern you know, so each digit is a chunk of its own. Nine chunks is more than the store can hold. The figure shows the same idea with an eleven-digit phone number.

afterFigure.text: Read as eleven separate digits, the number is far over the limit. Read as groups of five, three and three, it makes three chunks and fits with room to spare. The capacity is the same in both pictures. Only the number of chunks needed has changed.

lead.text: Nine unrelated digits are read once, with no way to group them. Each digit is its own chunk, and the capacity is four chunks.

If the limit is on chunks, and a chunk is whatever you know as one unit, there is a way to fit more into the same space: make each chunk carry more. This is chunking, the grouping of items into units you already know. A reader who knows the acronyms CD and TV sees the four letters CDTV as two chunks. Scramble them into DCVT and each letter becomes a chunk of its own, four in all.

The limit of about four chunks is the same for everyone. What differs is how much each chunk contains. Four single-letter chunks hold four letters. Four chunks that are each a three-letter acronym hold twelve.
Card numbers and postcodes are written in groups for this reason. The groups split a long string into pieces small enough to carry, and people who learn the groups well can carry them without effort.
Chunks depend on what the reader already knows. Count the pieces this reader would hold.

steps.headline: How a chess master remembers a board

lead.text: Chunking is easiest to see in experts. In the early 1970s William Chase and Herbert Simon showed a chess master and some weaker players a real game position for five seconds, then asked each of them to rebuild it from memory. The master put back far more of the pieces.

It would be easy to guess that masters simply have better memories. A second condition says otherwise. When the pieces were placed at random, as they never would be in a game, the master's advantage mostly disappeared. A master has seen so many real positions that a cluster of pieces, such as a castled king with the three pawns in front of it, is one familiar pattern. A weaker player sees the same cluster as separate pieces. With random placements the patterns are gone, and the master has nothing to chunk.
So the master's working memory is ordinary, with the same limit of about four chunks. The difference lies in how much each chunk holds. The figure shows a simplified position of twelve pieces.

afterFigure.text: The master sees the twelve pieces as three patterns, which fit in a store of four chunks. The novice sees twelve single pieces, which overflow it.

lead.text: Now take a larger, real position of 20 pieces. The master recalls all of it, grouped into 4 chunks.

So far working memory has been a single store with a size. In 1974 the psychologists Alan Baddeley and Graham Hitch argued that it is better described as a small team of parts, each handling a different kind of material, with a controller above them. The model has been revised since, but its main parts have held up.

The phonological loop holds sounds and words. It is the voice in your head that repeats a phone number to keep it alive. The visuospatial sketchpad holds images and positions, such as the layout of a room or the route you are about to walk. The episodic buffer ties material from these parts and from long-term memory into one scene or story. Above them sits the central executive, which stores nothing itself. It directs attention and decides what to hold and what to drop.

Separate parts explain something a single store cannot. Two jobs that use different parts, such as remembering a phone number and picturing a route, interfere with each other very little. Two jobs that use the same part, such as holding two phone numbers at once, interfere a great deal.
Each part of the model has its own job, and one of them does not hold material at all.
People recalled short lists of words in the order they heard them. Some lists sounded alike, such as man, cat, map. Others did not, such as pit, day, cow.

lesson.orientation: Estimate working-memory capacity in chunks and use knowledge to make the chunks bigger.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: Read each list once, look away for ten seconds, then say it back. List A: 4 9 1 7 2 8 5 3 6. List B: 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 9.

Most people find list B easy and list A a struggle, with the early digits slipping away by the fifth or sixth. Yet both lists are nine digits long, and they contain exactly the same digits. They take the same time to read. The length cannot be what makes B easier.

This lesson tries to find out what it is. It starts with the short-term workspace that held those digits for ten seconds, and the limit on what fits in it. It then shows how knowledge stretches that limit, using a chess master as the best example, and ends by looking at how the workspace is organised inside.

intro.promise: By the end you'll estimate how many chunks you can hold, and show how knowledge makes each chunk bigger.

recap.keyIdea: Working memory holds about four chunks, and a chunk is whatever you already know as a unit. Knowledge makes chunks bigger, so expertise raises what you hold without raising the limit.

blocks.text: Back at the two lists, you found that nine unrelated digits overflow a four-chunk store by 5. Three familiar acronyms make three chunks, and a master who holds five pieces in each chunk keeps 20 pieces where a novice keeps 4. You also matched the muddling of similar-sounding words to the phonological loop.

recap.nextHook: Working memory holds things for seconds and then lets them go. The next lesson follows a memory you want to keep, starting with 100 new words, 60 of them still known a day later.

questions.prompt: A 16-digit card number is printed in groups of four. If each group becomes one chunk, how many chunks must be held?
hints: Each printed group becomes a single chunk.
Find how many groups of four make 16.
Divide 16 by the group size.
questions.onCorrect: Each printed group becomes one chunk, so sixteen digits become only a few chunks.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts the digits. Each group of four is one chunk.
That is the number of digits left after one group. Divide the digits by the size of a group.

questions.prompt: What is the strategy of organising items into meaningful groups so more fits in short-term memory called?
hints: The groups are called chunks.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Chunking: grouping items into units already known from long-term memory.

questions.onCorrect: Chunking groups items into units already known, so more fits within the same limit.

misconceptions.feedback: Rehearsal repeats items. The strategy asked about groups them into units.

questions.prompt: A novice holds one piece per chunk and a master holds five. With a capacity of four chunks, how many more pieces can the master hold?
hints: Find how many pieces each person holds in four chunks.
The novice holds one piece in each chunk.
Subtract the novice's total from the master's.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The master holds 4 × 5 = 20 pieces, the novice 4 × 1 = 4. The difference is 16.

questions.onCorrect: Same capacity, richer chunks: four chunks of five pieces hold far more than four single pieces.

misconceptions.feedback: That is how many the master holds. The question asks how many more than the novice.
That is how many the novice holds, not the difference.

questions.prompt: Why is list B so much easier to hold?
hints: Count the digits in each list.
What do you already know about the order 1 to 9?

acceptedIdeas: You know its pattern, so you hold it as one thing, not nine.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: You already know the pattern, so you hold it as one familiar unit instead of nine separate digits.

choices.label: You know its pattern, so you hold it as one thing, not nine.

questions.onCorrect: Knowledge turns many items into one. You discovered chunking before it had a name.

misconceptions.feedback: Both lists have nine digits, and their size makes no difference to memory.
Both lists have nine digits. The difference is in what you already know.

hints: A chunk depends on what the person knows.

acceptedIdeas: A unit that you already know
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A chunk is a unit already stored in long-term memory, whatever its size.

choices.label: A group of exactly seven items
A unit that you already know

questions.onCorrect: A chunk is whatever you already know as a unit: a letter for one reader, a word for another.

misconceptions.feedback: A single digit is a chunk only if you know nothing that links it to others.
Chunks vary in size. The limit is on how many, not how many items.

questions.prompt: How many digits exceed the limit?
hints: Each separate digit counts as one chunk.
Compare the number of chunks with the capacity.
Subtract the capacity from the number of digits.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Nine chunks against a capacity of four leaves 9 − 4 = 5 beyond the limit.

questions.onCorrect: Nine chunks against a capacity of four leaves the difference beyond the limit.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts every digit. Only those beyond what the store can hold exceed the limit.
That is the capacity. The question asks how many are over it.

questions.prompt: A reader knows the acronyms BBC, NHS and USA. How many chunks is the string BBCNHSUSA for this reader?
hints: Which parts of the string does the reader already know?
Each known acronym is one chunk.
Count the acronyms.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: BBC, NHS and USA are three known units, so three chunks.

questions.onCorrect: Known acronyms make three chunks. Scrambled, the same letters would be nine separate chunks.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts every letter. The reader holds each known acronym as one unit.
That treats the whole string as one unit. The reader knows three separate acronyms.

questions.prompt: How many more letters can they hold by chunking than by storing one letter per chunk?
hints: Find how many letters fit when each chunk is an acronym.
Find how many fit when each chunk is one letter.
Subtract the second from the first.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Four acronym chunks hold 12 letters; four single-letter chunks hold 4; the gain is 8.

questions.onCorrect: Each chunk holds a whole acronym, so the same four chunks carry far more letters.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number held by chunking. The question asks for the extra over one letter per chunk.
That is how many letters fit without chunking. Find the gain over that.

questions.prompt: A chess master recalls a 20-piece position as 4 chunks. On average, how many pieces are in each chunk?
hints: Average means total pieces shared equally across chunks.
There are 20 pieces in the position.
Divide by the number of chunks.
questions.onCorrect: The master's chunks are rich, with several pieces in each. Capacity stays ordinary.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of chunks. The question asks how many pieces each one holds.
That subtracts instead of sharing the pieces out equally.

questions.prompt: Which part of the model directs attention among the others?
hints: Which part is a controller rather than a store?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The central executive directs attention among the other parts.

questions.onCorrect: The central executive is the controller that directs attention. The others store material.

misconceptions.feedback: The sketchpad stores images and positions. It does not direct attention.
The buffer links stored material. Directing attention is another job.

questions.prompt: Lists of similar-sounding words are harder to recall in order. Which part of Baddeley and Hitch's working-memory model does this point to?
hints: The interference comes from sound.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The phonological loop stores speech-based codes, so similar sounds interfere with one another.

questions.onCorrect: Similar sounds interfere in the speech-based store, so similar-sounding words are recalled worse.

misconceptions.feedback: The sketchpad holds images and positions, not sound.
The central executive directs attention. It does not store sound.
The episodic buffer links the other parts. The interference here comes from sound.
